stem: Pyruvate dehydrogenase processing yields a two-carbon unit that enters the citric acid cycle. What is that product called?

options.label: A
options.explanation: OpenStax names the pyruvate-derived compound acetyl CoA.
options.misconception: None; the compound formed is acetyl CoA.

options.label: B
options.explanation: It is the cycle partner, not the pyruvate product.
options.misconception: Oxaloacetate accepts the acetyl group.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not the immediate pyruvate dehydrogenase product.
options.misconception: A later cycle intermediate.

options.label: D
options.explanation: PEP precedes pyruvate in glycolysis.
options.misconception: A glycolytic intermediate upstream of pyruvate.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate makes citrate.
options.misconception: Citrate is the first condensation product after acetyl-CoA entry.

explanation: Learning objective: identify acetyl-CoA as the pyruvate-derived citric-cycle entry unit.

stem: An allosteric inhibitor typically binds where on the enzyme?

options.label: A
options.text: Only to ribosomal RNA in the cytosol
options.explanation: Allostery here is protein-ligand regulation.
options.misconception: Wrong macromolecule class.

options.label: B
options.text: At a regulatory site away from catalysis
options.explanation: OpenStax describes an allosteric site that still prevents substrate binding at the active site.
options.misconception: None; allosteric ligands bind elsewhere and reshape function.

options.label: C
options.text: First destroys the substrate in solution
options.explanation: Classic allostery is conformational on the enzyme.
options.misconception: Not required for classic allosteric control.

options.label: D
options.text: Covalently on the catalytic nucleophile only
options.explanation: Allosteric sites are separate regulatory pockets.
options.misconception: Describes some irreversible covalent inhibitors.

options.label: E
options.text: Only to oxygen within complex IV
options.explanation: Not general enzyme allostery.
options.misconception: Category error from electron transport.

explanation: Learning objective: allosteric inhibitors bind away from the active site.

stem: What directly powers ATP formation during oxidative phosphorylation?

options.label: A
options.text: Spontaneous ADP joining without a gradient
options.explanation: The gradient is required.
options.misconception: Without proton-motive force, synthesis stalls.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct phosphate transfer from NADH to ADP
options.explanation: NADH donates electrons; the proton current drives synthesis.
options.misconception: NADH does not substrate-level phosphorylate ADP here.

options.label: C
options.text: Hydrogen-ion flow through the F0-F1 complex
options.explanation: OpenStax: hydrogen-ion current powers ATP synthase phosphorylation of ADP.
options.misconception: None; proton flux drives the synthase.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Chemiosmosis here is redox-driven.
options.misconception: Animal mitochondria are not photosynthetic.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Most aerobic ATP is chemiosmotic.
options.misconception: That is glycolysis/TCA substrate-level ATP.

explanation: Learning objective: chemiosmotic proton flow drives ATP synthase.

stem: The central dogma of molecular biology describes macromolecular information flow as which sequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Glucose to glycogen as the usual forward path
options.explanation: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Metabolism, not genetic flow.

options.label: B
options.text: Protein to RNA to DNA as the usual forward path
options.explanation: Forward flow is DNA to RNA to protein.
options.misconception: That reverses the dogma.

options.label: C
options.text: Lipid to carbohydrate as the usual forward path
options.explanation: Not the dogma; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Wrong macromolecules.

options.label: D
options.text: DNA to RNA to protein as the usual forward path
options.explanation: OpenStax: central dogma of DNA-protein synthesis.
options.misconception: None; that is the central dogma summary.

options.label: E
options.text: ATP to heat as the usual forward path
options.explanation: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Energy story, not sequence flow.

explanation: Learning objective: central dogma links DNA to protein synthesis.

stem: Per turn of the citric acid cycle, which reduced electron carriers are formed according to the standard textbook accounting?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Citric cycle uses NAD+/FAD.
options.misconception: Mixes PPP carriers with TCA.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Each turn forms multiple NADH plus FADH2.
options.misconception: Under-counts NADH and omits FADH2.

options.label: C
options.explanation: FADH2 yield is one per turn.
options.misconception: Swaps NADH/FADH2 counts.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Dehydrogenases generate NADH/FADH2.
options.misconception: Ignores dehydrogenase steps.

options.label: E
options.explanation: OpenStax: each turn forms three NADH and one FADH2.
options.misconception: None; that is the per-turn yield.

explanation: Learning objective: recall citric-cycle reduced-carrier yield per turn.

stem: In competitive inhibition, how does the inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?

options.label: A
options.text: It competes with substrate for active-site binding
options.explanation: OpenStax: the inhibitor competes with substrate for active-site binding.
options.misconception: None; competitive inhibitors bind the active site.

options.label: B
options.text: It binds DNA enhancers and blocks transcription
options.explanation: Different mechanism; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Transcriptional regulation, not catalytic inhibition.

options.label: C
options.text: It digests the enzyme into free amino acids
options.explanation: Competitive inhibition is binding competition.
options.misconception: That would be proteolysis, not classic competition.

options.label: D
options.text: It pumps protons to starve ATP synthesis
options.explanation: Not enzyme active-site competition.
options.misconception: Wrong physiologic system.

options.label: E
options.text: It replaces mRNA so the enzyme is not produced
options.explanation: Different timescale; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Expression control, not catalytic inhibition.

explanation: Learning objective: competitive inhibitors vie for the active site.

stem: Watson and Crick proposed which structural description of DNA?

options.label: A
options.text: A hollow tube made of membrane lipids
options.explanation: Irrelevant; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Membrane fantasy — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: B
options.text: Two strands twisted into a helix
options.explanation: OpenStax recounts two strands twisted around each other.
options.misconception: None; DNA is a double helix.

options.label: C
options.text: One peptide strand in an alpha coil
options.explanation: DNA is nucleic acid; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Confuses protein structure with DNA.

options.label: D
options.explanation: DNA is polynucleotide.
options.misconception: Wrong polymer class — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Two nucleic-acid strands.
options.misconception: Not the Watson-Crick model.

explanation: Learning objective: DNA is a double helix.

stem: What critical catalytic task do almost all enzymes perform inside cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Replace ATP as the universal energy currency
options.explanation: Enzymes catalyze its use.
options.misconception: ATP remains the phosphoryl currency.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the equilibrium constant of reactions
options.explanation: Catalysis is kinetic.
options.misconception: Enzymes speed rates; they do not alter delta-G equilibrium.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower the activation energies of chemical reactions
options.explanation: OpenStax: enzymes lower activation energies of cellular reactions.
options.misconception: None; enzymes lower activation energies.

options.label: D
options.text: Supply the net free energy for endergonic processes without coupling
options.explanation: Enzymes do not create energy.
options.misconception: Endergonic work still needs energetic coupling.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Enzymes are reaction-specific.
options.misconception: Nonsense category error.

explanation: Learning objective: enzymes lower activation energy.

stem: During electron transport in mitochondria, what happens to protons that enables chemiosmotic ATP synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: They freely equilibrate across an unsealed outer membrane only
options.explanation: Complexes pump across the inner membrane.
options.misconception: Outer membrane is porous; the relevant barrier is the inner membrane.

options.label: B
options.text: They diffuse into the nucleus to activate transcription
options.explanation: Nuclear signaling is separate.
options.misconception: No such ETC coupling.

options.label: C
options.text: They are consumed as the carbon skeleton of glucose
options.explanation: CO2 carbons come from substrate carbons.
options.misconception: Protons are not incorporated into CO2 carbon.

options.label: D
options.text: They are pumped from the matrix to the intermembrane space
options.explanation: OpenStax: protons are pumped from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space.
options.misconception: None; proton pumping creates the intermembrane gradient.

options.label: E
options.text: They are stored inside ATP before hydrolysis
options.explanation: The proton gradient is across the membrane.
options.misconception: ATP stores phosphoryl transfer energy, not a proton pool.

explanation: Learning objective: ETC pumps protons out of the matrix.

stem: If aerobic respiration does not occur, why must NADH be reoxidized to NAD+?

options.label: A
options.text: ATP synthase consumes NADH as its substrate
options.explanation: NADH feeds the ETC when available.
options.misconception: ATP synthase uses ADP+Pi and proton flow.

options.label: B
options.text: Oxygen can oxidize glucose without any carriers
options.explanation: Carrier regeneration is the point.
options.misconception: Oxygen is not a direct glycolytic oxidant.

options.label: C
options.text: NADH must become NADPH for biosynthesis only
options.explanation: The issue is NAD+ availability for GAPDH.
options.misconception: Wrong cofactor story.

options.label: D
options.text: NAD+ is needed only to build glycogen stores
options.explanation: Fermentation sustains sugar breakdown.
options.misconception: Not the described bottleneck.

options.label: E
options.text: NAD+ must be regenerated as an electron carrier
options.explanation: OpenStax: NADH must be reoxidized to NAD+ for reuse as an electron carrier so glycolysis can continue.
options.misconception: None; NAD+ is needed when the ETC is unavailable.

explanation: Learning objective: fermentation regenerates NAD+ for glycolysis.

stem: What is glycogen in animals?

options.label: A
options.text: A polymer of glucose used for energy storage
options.explanation: OpenStax: glycogen, a polymer of glucose, is an energy storage molecule in animals.
options.misconception: None; glycogen is a glucose polymer energy store.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Cellulose is plant fiber.
options.misconception: Humans do not store cellulose as glycogen.

options.label: C
options.text: A mitochondrial electron carrier like ubiquinone
options.explanation: Glycogen is cytosolic storage.
options.misconception: Wrong compartment/function.

options.label: D
options.text: A protein hormone from the pancreas
options.explanation: Glycogen is a polysaccharide.
options.misconception: Confuses glycogen with glucagon/insulin.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Different molecule class.
options.misconception: That would be NADH — does not match the cited teaching point.

explanation: Learning objective: glycogen = animal glucose storage polymer.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain for 45 minutes. Electrocardiography shows ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V4, and cardiac catheterization confirms occlusion of the left anterior descending artery. Biopsy of the ischemic myocardium reveals depleted mitochondrial ATP and accumulating lactate despite continued glucose uptake.

Which of the following best explains why substrate-level ATP production can briefly continue in this tissue without oxygen?

options.label: A
options.text: Glycolysis proceeds in the cytosol and does not require oxygen
options.explanation: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol and can proceed without oxygen; under ischemia it continues briefly to supply substrate-level ATP while mitochondria cannot run oxidative phosphorylation.
options.misconception: None; glycolysis is anaerobic and cytosolic.

options.label: B
options.text: Glycolysis relocates into mitochondria when oxygen delivery falls
options.explanation: Glycolysis remains cytosolic; mitochondria run the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, which fail without oxygen.
options.misconception: A compartment shift is being invented for anaerobiosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Hexokinase begins to consume oxygen as an alternative substrate
options.explanation: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose with ATP; it does not use oxygen, and ischemia does not convert it into an oxidase.
options.misconception: The glucose-trapping enzyme is being given a respiratory role.

options.label: D
options.text: PFK stops so that all ATP is spared for ion pumps
options.explanation: PFK regulation modulates glycolytic rate; the reason ATP can still be made without O2 is that glycolysis itself is anaerobic, not that PFK stops.
options.misconception: Regulatory shutdown is being treated as the reason ATP continues.

options.label: E
options.text: Myosin ATPase reverses to generate ATP from ADP
options.explanation: Myosin hydrolyzes ATP; it does not reverse to synthesize ATP during ischemia—the brief ATP comes from cytosolic glycolysis.
options.misconception: Contractile ATPase is being cast as an ATP synthase.

explanation: Learning objective: apply anaerobic glycolysis in ischemia. Glycolysis is cytoplasmic and oxygen-independent, so it can continue briefly when mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation fails.

stem: Which statement best describes glycolysis with respect to oxygen requirement and cellular location in eukaryotes?

options.label: A
options.text: It requires molecular oxygen in the mitochondrial matrix
options.explanation: Oxygen is the terminal acceptor of the electron transport chain, not a glycolytic substrate.
options.misconception: Confuses glycolysis with oxidative phosphorylation.

options.label: B
options.text: It does not use oxygen directly and occurs in the cytoplasm
options.explanation: OpenStax states glycolysis is termed anaerobic and takes place in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.
options.misconception: None; glycolysis is anaerobic and cytosolic.

options.label: C
options.text: It occurs only on the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.explanation: Inner-membrane complexes belong to oxidative phosphorylation.
options.misconception: Misplaces the pathway on the ETC membrane.

options.label: D
options.text: It is strictly aerobic and mitochondrial
options.explanation: Glycolysis proceeds without direct O2 use in the cytosol.
options.misconception: Opposite of the actual oxygen independence and location.

options.label: E
options.text: It occurs in the nucleus during S phase
options.explanation: Nucleotide metabolism is separate from glycolytic sugar cleavage.
options.misconception: Invented nuclear localization.

explanation: Learning objective: place glycolysis as anaerobic cytoplasmic metabolism.

stem: In eukaryotic cytoplasm, what are the net carbon products of glycolysis starting from one glucose before mitochondrial oxidation?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Full oxidation to six CO2 requires pyruvate processing plus citric acid cycle turns.
options.misconception: Jumps to complete aerobic oxidation of glucose.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Acetyl-CoA forms after pyruvate enters mitochondria and is processed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase path.
options.misconception: Skips the mitochondrial pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA step.

options.label: C
options.explanation: OpenStax Biology notes glycolysis begins with glucose and produces two pyruvate molecules (plus ATP and NADH carriers).
options.misconception: None; glycolysis cleaves glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates.

options.label: D
options.explanation: CO2 release occurs during pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle, not glycolysis itself.
options.misconception: Confuses glycolysis with pyruvate dehydrogenase oxidative decarboxylation.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Lactate appears only if NADH is reoxidized by fermentation rather than the electron transport chain.
options.misconception: Assumes obligatory lactic fermentation.

explanation: Learning objective: recall glycolysis carbon products. Glycolysis is anaerobic and cytosolic; it yields two pyruvates.

stem: Hexokinase catalyzes the first committed trapping step of glycolysis. What does it do to glucose?

options.label: A
options.explanation: GLUT facilitators move glucose; hexokinase modifies it.
options.misconception: Transport is not an enzymatic phosphorylation.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Cleavage occurs after fructose-1,6-bisphosphate formation.
options.misconception: That is later aldolase chemistry.

options.label: C
options.explanation: That oxidative step is not the hexokinase reaction.
options.misconception: Describes glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in PPP.

options.label: D
options.explanation: OpenStax: hexokinase phosphorylates glucose using ATP, producing glucose-6-phosphate.
options.misconception: None; hexokinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to glucose.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Polymer storage is separate from glycolytic entry.
options.misconception: Glycogen synthase territory.

explanation: Learning objective: hexokinase phosphorylates glucose with ATP.

stem: Which enzyme regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate under anaerobic conditions?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Citric-cycle entry, not lactate.
options.misconception: Condenses acetyl-CoA with OAA.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not the fermentation enzyme.
options.misconception: Makes acetyl-CoA aerobically.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Upstream of pyruvate.
options.misconception: Phosphorylates glucose.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not a fermentation NAD+ salvage enzyme.
options.misconception: Makes ATP from proton flow.

options.label: E
options.explanation: OpenStax identifies lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) for this reaction.
options.misconception: None; LDH reduces pyruvate with NADH.

explanation: Learning objective: LDH performs lactic fermentation.

stem: In aerobic mitochondrial electron transport, what is the final electron acceptor?

options.label: A
options.explanation: OpenStax: oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain.
options.misconception: None; oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Electrons continue to complex IV and O2.
options.misconception: Cytochrome c is an intermediate carrier.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Respiration consumes O2.
options.misconception: That is photosynthetic O2 production, opposite direction.

options.label: D
options.explanation: O2 becomes water after accepting electrons.
options.misconception: CO2 is a carbon waste of decarboxylation, not an ETC acceptor.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Terminal acceptor is O2.
options.misconception: NAD+ accepts electrons in dehydrogenases earlier, not at complex IV terminus.

explanation: Learning objective: O2 is the terminal ETC acceptor.

stem: When DNA damage is detected, what does normal p53 do according to the OpenStax cancer chapter?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: ETC, not p53 — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: B
options.explanation: OpenStax: if damage is detected, p53 triggers repair mechanisms.
options.misconception: None; damaged DNA detection leads p53 to trigger repair.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Psychology confusion.

options.label: D
options.explanation: p53 is a checkpoint/tumor-suppressor response.
options.misconception: Wrong pathway — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: PDH, not p53 — does not match the cited teaching point.

explanation: Learning objective: p53 responds to damage by triggering repair.

stem: Which statement about glycolytic regulation matches the OpenStax account?

options.label: A
options.text: Oxygen level is the sole metabolic input
options.explanation: Multiple inputs exist.
options.misconception: Oxygen affects aerobic fate, but nucleotide regulators also act.

options.label: B
options.text: There are no regulated enzymatic steps
options.explanation: Regulation concentrates at committed steps.
options.misconception: False; key steps are control points.

options.label: C
options.text: A few key enzymatic steps set the pace
options.explanation: OpenStax: glycolysis is primarily regulated at three key enzymatic steps.
options.misconception: None; regulation focuses on key steps.

options.label: D
options.text: Only ATP synthase sets the sugar-breakdown rate
options.explanation: Glycolysis has its own control enzymes.
options.misconception: ATP synthase is mitochondrial oxphos.

options.label: E
options.text: DNA sequence is rewritten after every meal
options.explanation: Allosteric/hormonal control is faster.
options.misconception: Gene sequence does not flip each meal.

explanation: Learning objective: glycolysis is regulated at key enzymatic steps.

stem: What are proto-oncogenes?

options.label: A
options.text: Genes that only trigger apoptosis programs
options.explanation: Opposite class; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Overlaps tumor-suppressor roles like p53.

options.label: B
options.text: Ribosomal RNA molecules with no protein product
options.explanation: They are typically protein-coding genes.
options.misconception: Wrong molecule class.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Genes, not nutrients.
options.misconception: Nonsense — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: D
options.explanation: OpenStax: genes for positive cell-cycle regulators are called proto-oncogenes.
options.misconception: None; they encode positive regulators.

options.label: E
options.text: Viral capsids that digest chromosomal DNA
options.explanation: Proto-oncogenes are cellular genes.
options.misconception: Wrong concept for this stem; does not match the cited passage.

explanation: Learning objective: proto-oncogenes are positive cell-cycle regulator genes.

stem: After glycolysis in a eukaryotic cell with oxygen available, where are the pyruvate molecules transported next?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Glycosylation substrates are nucleotide sugars.
options.misconception: Golgi processes proteins, not pyruvate oxidation.

options.label: B
options.text: Out of the cell as lactate only
options.explanation: Aerobic cells oxidize pyruvate in mitochondria.
options.misconception: Lactate export is a fermentation alternative, not the aerobic default.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Transcription uses NTPs, not pyruvate import.
options.misconception: Pyruvate is not a nuclear metabolite for gene expression.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Fatty-acid beta-oxidation can use peroxisomes/mitochondria; pyruvate goes to mitochondria.
options.misconception: Wrong organelle and pathway.

options.label: E
options.explanation: OpenStax: pyruvate produced at the end of glycolysis is transported into the mitochondria when oxygen is available.
options.misconception: None; pyruvate is transported into mitochondria.

explanation: Learning objective: link glycolysis products to mitochondrial oxidation.

stem: During DNA replication, what role does each parental chain play?

options.label: A
options.text: It templates a new complementary chain
options.explanation: OpenStax: each strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand.
options.misconception: None; each parental chain templates a complement.

options.label: B
options.text: It binds oxygen as the terminal acceptor
options.explanation: Unrelated to replication.
options.misconception: ETC confusion — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: C
options.text: It is discarded and replaced by RNA only
options.explanation: Semiconservative copying uses each chain.
options.misconception: Parental chains remain as templates.

options.label: D
options.text: It is converted into glycogen stores
options.explanation: Nucleic acid remains nucleic acid.
options.misconception: Category error — does not match the cited teaching point.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Wrong process; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: That is ribosomal peptidyl transferase.

explanation: Learning objective: parental DNA strands are templates.

stem: Relative to glycogen, triglycerides in animals are best described as which store?

options.label: A
options.explanation: This option does not match the cited source passage for the stem.
options.misconception: That is hemoglobin/myoglobin territory.

options.label: B
options.text: Long-term caloric reserve in adipose tissue
options.explanation: OpenStax describes triglycerides as long-term energy storage in animals.
options.misconception: None; fats are long-term storage.

options.label: C
options.explanation: They are long-term fuel stores.
options.misconception: Lipids are not neurotransmitters here.

options.label: D
options.text: The only anaerobic ATP source in muscle
options.explanation: Not anaerobic; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: Fat oxidation is aerobic.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
options.misconception: DNA uses phosphodiester sugars/bases.

explanation: Learning objective: triglycerides are long-term energy stores.

stem: In the genetic code, what is the nucleotide triplet that specifies an amino acid called?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Replication, not coding unit name.
options.misconception: Lagging-strand DNA pieces.

options.label: B
options.explanation: This option does not match the cited source passage for the stem.
options.misconception: General binder term, not the code unit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: OpenStax refers to the triplet codon.
options.misconception: None; the triplet is a codon.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Not the amino-acid specifier name.
options.misconception: Introns are intervening sequences removed from pre-mRNA.

options.label: E
options.explanation: This option does not match the cited source passage for the stem.
options.misconception: Histones package DNA.

explanation: Learning objective: codon = nucleotide triplet coding an amino acid.

stem:
In a hypothetical cell system, glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase using ATP. A variant markedly reduces that enzyme's activity. Later reactions function normally, and investigators can introduce metabolites directly into the relevant compartment.

Which of the following interventions most directly bypasses the defective conversion while supplying its downstream pathway?

options.label: A
options.text: Supply glucose-6-phosphate directly to the cell system
options.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate is the product of the impaired reaction. Direct delivery supplies the next pathway step without requiring the defective hexokinase conversion to function first.
options.misconception: No misconception: Directly supplying the reaction product bypasses the impaired conversion in this model.

options.label: B
options.text: Supply additional glucose directly to the cell system
options.explanation: Glucose is the substrate upstream of the impaired conversion. Increasing its availability does not bypass the requirement for hexokinase to form the downstream metabolite.
options.misconception: Confuses adding more upstream substrate with bypassing the enzyme required to convert it.

options.label: C
options.text: Supply a competing active-site ligand to hexokinase
options.explanation: An active-site competitor opposes substrate access rather than supplying the missing product. It therefore does not provide a bypass around the impaired enzymatic conversion.
options.misconception: Treats an active-site competitor as a source of the missing downstream product.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove glucose-6-phosphate from the cell system
options.explanation: Removing the product further reduces material available for the downstream reactions. It acts in the opposite direction from the requested restoration of pathway input.
options.misconception: Removes the downstream input while attempting to restore supply to later pathway reactions.

options.label: E
options.text: Remove the ATP available to the cell system
options.explanation: The specified hexokinase reaction consumes ATP. Removing this reactant would add a limitation to conversion rather than bypass the existing defect with its product.
options.misconception: Treats withdrawal of a required reactant as a bypass around the defective conversion.

explanation: Learning objective: select a bypass at the product side of an enzymatic block. Supplying the immediate product avoids the impaired conversion; supplying substrate or an inhibitor does not achieve that bypass.

stem:
A hypothetical isolated pathway is X → Y → Z. Enzyme 1 converts X to Y, and enzyme 2 converts Y to Z; there are no alternative routes. After a sequence variant reduces one enzyme's function, X accumulates while Y and Z fall.

Which of the following best explains this pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced activity of enzyme 2 converting Y to Z
options.explanation: A block at the second conversion would restrict consumption of Y. That does not explain the stated combination of accumulating X with depletion of Y.
options.misconception: Places the block after the depleted intermediate instead of before its impaired formation.

options.label: B
options.text: Increased activity of enzyme 1 converting X to Y
options.explanation: Increasing the first conversion would favor X consumption and Y formation. That direction conflicts with the measured accumulation of X and reduction of downstream products.
options.misconception: Predicts substrate accumulation from increasing the reaction that consumes that substrate.

options.label: C
options.text: Increased activity of enzyme 2 converting Y to Z
options.explanation: Enhanced conversion of Y to Z does not explain why Z is depleted. It also does not directly account for accumulation before the first reaction.
options.misconception: Uses increased conversion into the final product to explain depletion of that same product.

options.label: D
options.text: Unchanged activity of both enzymes in the pathway
options.explanation: The experiment attributes the concentration shift to reduced enzyme function and excludes alternative routes. Preserving both activities leaves the specified pathway interruption unexplained in this model.
options.misconception: Preserves both enzyme activities despite the stated enzyme defect and exclusion of alternative routes.

options.label: E
options.text: Reduced activity of enzyme 1 converting X to Y
options.explanation: Blocking the first conversion permits X to accumulate while limiting Y formation. The shortage of Y then also restricts the downstream formation of Z.
options.misconception: No misconception: Blocking the first reaction allows its substrate to accumulate and restricts both downstream products.

explanation: Learning objective: localize a pathway interruption using both substrate accumulation and product depletion. The earliest blocked conversion determines which metabolite rises and which downstream metabolites become scarce.

evidence.title: Promoting Safe and Effective Genetic Testing in the United States - Glossary

stem:
In a study model, event X has probability 0.20 and event Y has probability 0.30. The model explicitly assumes the two events are independent.

Which of the following probabilities should it assign to both events occurring in the same participant?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Zero would mean the events cannot occur together. Independence instead permits joint occurrence and specifies that its probability equals the product of the two individual probabilities.
options.misconception: Confuses independence with events that cannot occur together.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Subtracting the individual probabilities gives 0.10 but does not calculate their joint occurrence. For independent events, the appropriate operation is multiplication rather than subtraction.
options.misconception: Subtracts marginal probabilities instead of multiplying them for the joint event.

options.label: C
options.explanation: This is the probability of event X alone. Requiring event Y to occur as well changes the probability to the product 0.20 × 0.30.
options.misconception: Uses the probability of X alone without also requiring Y.

options.label: D
options.explanation: For independent events, the joint probability is the product of their individual probabilities. Multiplying 0.20 by 0.30 gives 0.06, or a 6% chance of both.
options.misconception: No misconception: independent joint probability is the product of the marginals.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Adding the individual probabilities does not calculate both events occurring. The independent joint-event calculation uses multiplication; summing the probabilities answers a different and incomplete probability question.
options.misconception: Adds marginal probabilities to estimate both events occurring.

explanation:
Learning objective: Apply the product rule to a joint event only when independence is established or explicitly assumed.

For independent events, the joint probability is the product of their individual probabilities. Multiplying 0.20 by 0.30 gives 0.06, or a 6% chance of both.

stem:
A trial compares the mean change in a measurement between a new intervention and a control. The planned statistical test evaluates whether the population means differ.

Which of the following statements is the null hypothesis for this comparison?

options.label: A
options.text: The intervention produces a larger population mean change
options.explanation: A larger mean change is a directional difference, rather than the no-difference claim being tested. It describes one possible alternative to equal population mean changes.
options.misconception: Substitutes a directional increase for the population no-difference claim.

options.label: B
options.text: The intervention produces a smaller population mean change
options.explanation: A smaller mean change is also a directional difference. The null hypothesis for the stated comparison specifies equal population mean changes rather than choosing either direction.
options.misconception: Substitutes a directional decrease for equality of population means.

options.label: C
options.text: The difference in population mean changes is nonzero
options.explanation: A nonzero difference is the two-sided alternative hypothesis for this comparison. The null retains equality of the population mean changes, corresponding to a difference of zero.
options.misconception: Confuses the two-sided alternative with the no-difference null.

options.label: D
options.text: The difference in population mean changes is exactly zero
options.explanation: For this comparison, the null hypothesis states that the two population mean changes are equal. A difference of zero expresses that no-difference claim on the measurement scale.
options.misconception: No misconception: this comparison tests a zero population mean difference.

options.label: E
options.text: The difference in sample mean changes is exactly zero
options.explanation: This statement concerns the particular sample rather than the population claim being tested. The null hypothesis is equality of population means, not a requirement that observed sample means match.
options.misconception: Confuses a population hypothesis with equality of observed sample means.

explanation:
Learning objective: Distinguish a population no-difference hypothesis from the observed difference in a trial sample.

For this comparison, the null hypothesis states that the two population mean changes are equal. A difference of zero expresses that no-difference claim on the measurement scale.

stem:
A screening program contacts everyone with a positive result. Before confirmatory testing, the program wants to estimate the fraction of these people who actually have the condition.

Which of the following quantities answers that question?

options.label: A
options.text: True positive results divided by all positive results
options.explanation: Positive predictive value uses the positive-test group as its denominator. It describes the fraction of those positive results that represent actual disease, which is the program’s question.
options.misconception: No misconception: PPV counts true positives among all positive results.

options.label: B
options.text: True cases detected divided by all people with disease
options.explanation: This describes sensitivity, the fraction of actual cases the screening test detects. It starts with people known to have disease, rather than the group contacted after positive results.
options.misconception: Confuses detection among actual cases with disease among positive results.

options.label: C
options.text: True negatives divided by all people without disease
options.explanation: This describes specificity, the fraction of disease-free people correctly testing negative. It does not estimate the fraction of positive results that correspond to actual disease.
options.misconception: Substitutes disease-free negative classification for positive predictive value.

options.label: D
options.text: False positive results divided by people without disease
options.explanation: This describes false-positive results among people without disease. The requested quantity instead starts with everyone testing positive and asks how many of them truly have disease.
options.misconception: Uses false positives among noncases instead of true disease among positives.

options.label: E
options.text: All people with disease divided by everyone screened
options.explanation: This describes disease frequency in the screened population. Positive predictive value instead restricts the denominator to positive results, rather than including everyone who was screened.
options.misconception: Substitutes whole-population disease frequency for the positive-test fraction.

explanation:
Learning objective: Choose the positive-test denominator for positive predictive value before applying it to a screening table.

Positive predictive value uses the positive-test group as its denominator. It describes the fraction of those positive results that represent actual disease, which is the program’s question.

stem:
A study records two binary results for each participant: whether an exposure is present and whether an outcome occurs. Each combination is possible.

Which of the following sets is the sample space for one participant’s paired record?

options.label: A
options.text: Exposure present with outcome; exposure absent without outcome
options.explanation: This set contains the two matching combinations but omits the discordant combinations. A sample space must include every possible paired record, not only selected patterns.
options.misconception: Omits discordant exposure-outcome combinations from the possible outcomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Exposure and outcome; exposure only; outcome only; neither
options.explanation: There are four possible combinations of two binary results: both present, exposure alone, outcome alone and neither. This set includes every possible record described by the study.
options.misconception: No misconception: four joint combinations exhaust two binary observations.

options.label: C
options.text: Exposure present with outcome; exposure present without outcome
options.explanation: This set restricts attention to exposed participants and omits both possibilities for unexposed participants. It is a subset of the full sample space for one paired record.
options.misconception: Restricts the sample space to exposed participants.

options.label: D
options.text: Exposure absent with outcome; exposure absent without outcome
options.explanation: This set restricts attention to unexposed participants and omits both possibilities for exposed participants. The sample space must include all four combinations allowed by the study.
options.misconception: Restricts the sample space to unexposed participants.

options.label: E
options.text: Exposure present with outcome; exposure absent with outcome
options.explanation: This set restricts attention to participants with the outcome and omits those without it. The full sample space must also include both exposure states when the outcome is absent.
options.misconception: Omits both exposure states when the outcome is absent.

explanation:
Learning objective: Enumerate the sample space before assigning probabilities to joint exposure and outcome categories.

There are four possible combinations of two binary results: both present, exposure alone, outcome alone and neither. This set includes every possible record described by the study.

stem:
A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negative.

Which of the following ratios measures the fraction of actual cases that the test detects?

options.label: A
options.explanation: This ratio is specificity, since it counts true negatives among all people without disease. The requested detection fraction instead starts with the actual cases, represented by A and C.
options.misconception: Uses the specificity formula when detection among actual cases is requested.

options.label: B
options.explanation: This ratio counts false positives among all positive results. It measures errors within the positive-test group rather than the fraction of actual cases successfully detected.
options.misconception: Counts false discoveries within positives instead of detected cases within disease.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Actual cases consist of true positives plus false negatives, A + C. The detected cases are A, so sensitivity is A divided by A + C.
options.misconception: No misconception: A plus C includes both detected and missed actual cases.

options.label: D
options.explanation: This ratio counts missed cases among all negative results. Sensitivity instead asks how many actual cases are detected, using the case group rather than negative results as the denominator.
options.misconception: Uses missed cases among negative results rather than detected cases among all cases.

options.label: E
options.explanation: This ratio is positive predictive value: true cases among all positive results. Sensitivity uses all actual cases, including missed cases, as its denominator instead.
options.misconception: Confuses the positive-result denominator with the actual-case denominator.

explanation:
Learning objective: Build the sensitivity denominator from true positives plus false negatives before interpreting screening results.

Actual cases consist of true positives plus false negatives, A + C. The detected cases are A, so sensitivity is A divided by A + C.

stem:
A surveillance team already knows which patients truly had a disease from an independent assessment. It asks how successfully a new case definition identifies those patients.

Which of the following quantities directly evaluates this goal?

options.label: A
options.text: False positive results divided by all positive results
options.explanation: This asks how many positive results are false alarms. Sensitivity instead starts with all people known to have disease and measures how many the definition detects.
options.misconception: Counts false alarms among positive results instead of detected actual cases.

options.label: B
options.text: True negative results divided by all negative results
options.explanation: This starts with negative results and measures how many are truly disease-free. The surveillance question instead concerns detection among the independently established group with disease.
options.misconception: Uses the negative-result denominator rather than the actual-case group.

options.label: C
options.text: True negative results divided by all disease-free patients
options.explanation: This is specificity: correctly excluding disease among people without it. Sensitivity uses the group with disease as the denominator and counts the cases detected.
options.misconception: Confuses exclusion among noncases with detection among cases.

options.label: D
options.text: True positive results divided by all people with disease
options.explanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases identified by a test or case definition. Divide the detected true cases by all independently established cases to evaluate this goal.
options.misconception: No misconception: sensitivity counts detected true cases among all actual cases.

options.label: E
options.text: True positive results divided by all positive results
options.explanation: This is positive predictive value, which evaluates whether positive results represent disease. Sensitivity evaluates how many actual cases are detected, so its denominator is all patients with disease.
options.misconception: Substitutes the PPV positive-result denominator for all people with disease.

explanation:
Learning objective: Identify the actual-case denominator for sensitivity before calculating case detection.

Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases identified by a test or case definition. Divide the detected true cases by all independently established cases to evaluate this goal.

stem:
A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negative.

Which of the following ratios measures correct negative classification among people without disease?

options.label: A
options.explanation: This ratio is sensitivity, since A and C together represent all actual cases. Specificity instead evaluates correct negative classification among the group without disease.
options.misconception: Uses the diseased-group sensitivity formula to assess disease-free classification.

options.label: B
options.explanation: This ratio is positive predictive value, since A and B together represent all positive results. The requested measure instead begins with people independently known to be disease-free.
options.misconception: Substitutes PPV for specificity by conditioning on positive results.

options.label: C
options.explanation: This ratio is the false-positive fraction among people without disease. It uses the right denominator but counts incorrect positive results rather than correct negative classifications.
options.misconception: Uses the correct noncase denominator but counts false positives as successes.

options.label: D
options.explanation: This ratio is the proportion of actual cases missed by the test. The question asks about correct exclusions among disease-free people, not missed detection among cases.
options.misconception: Counts missed actual cases instead of correctly excluded noncases.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Disease-free people consist of false positives and true negatives, B + D. Correct exclusions are D, so specificity is D divided by B + D.
options.misconception: No misconception: D counts true negatives within the disease-free group B plus D.

explanation:
Learning objective: Build the specificity denominator from false positives plus true negatives before evaluating screening errors.

Disease-free people consist of false positives and true negatives, B + D. Correct exclusions are D, so specificity is D divided by B + D.

stem:
A new surveillance rule is tested in a group confirmed to be free of the target disease. Investigators want to know how well the rule avoids incorrectly classifying these people as cases.

Which of the following quantities measures that ability?

options.label: A
options.text: Negative classifications divided by all disease-free people
options.explanation: Specificity measures correct negative classification among people who do not have the disease. The disease-free group is the denominator, and correctly negative results are the numerator.
options.misconception: No misconception: specificity counts correctly negative results among noncases.

options.label: B
options.text: Positive classifications divided by all disease-free people
options.explanation: This measures the false-positive fraction among people without disease. It complements specificity but counts errors, rather than the successful exclusions requested by the investigators.
options.misconception: Counts false-positive errors instead of successful disease exclusion.

options.label: C
options.text: True positive classifications divided by all positive results
options.explanation: This is positive predictive value, which starts with positive results. The specified study instead asks about correct classification within a group already known to be disease-free.
options.misconception: Confuses disease among positive results with negative classification of noncases.

options.label: D
options.text: True positive classifications divided by all people with disease
options.explanation: This is sensitivity, the detection fraction among people with disease. The investigators are assessing exclusion among people without disease, so a different denominator is required.
options.misconception: Substitutes detection among diseased people for exclusion among disease-free people.

options.label: E
options.text: True negative classifications divided by all negative results
options.explanation: This measures the fraction of negative results that are truly disease-free. Specificity instead includes all disease-free people, including those incorrectly classified as positive, in its denominator.
options.misconception: Uses negative results as the denominator instead of all disease-free people.

explanation:
Learning objective: Distinguish specificity from false-positive frequency and predictive value when evaluating a screening rule.

Specificity measures correct negative classification among people who do not have the disease. The disease-free group is the denominator, and correctly negative results are the numerator.

stem:
A screening test is evaluated in 1,000 people whose disease status is established independently. Of 100 people with disease, 90 test positive. Of 900 people without disease, 90 test positive.

Which of the following pairs gives the test sensitivity and the probability of disease among those testing positive?

options.label: A
options.text: Sensitivity 50%; probability of disease after a positive test 90%
options.explanation: Sensitivity uses all actual cases as its denominator, giving 90/100 rather than 90/180. The probability of disease among positive results uses all positive tests, giving 90/180 rather than 90/100.
options.misconception: Swaps the actual-case and positive-result denominators.

options.label: B
options.text: Sensitivity 90%; probability of disease after a positive test 50%
options.explanation: Sensitivity is 90 true positives divided by 100 people with disease, or 90%. Positive predictive value is 90 true positives divided by 180 positive results, or 50%.
options.misconception: No misconception: sensitivity and PPV condition on different groups.

options.label: C
options.text: Sensitivity 90%; probability of disease after a positive test 90%
options.explanation: The 90% sensitivity is correct, but it does not give the probability that a positive result represents disease. The positive group includes 90 people without disease, reducing that probability to 50%.
options.misconception: Treats sensitivity as the probability of disease after a positive result.

options.label: D
options.text: Sensitivity 10%; probability of disease after a positive test 50%
options.explanation: Ten percent is the proportion of actual cases missed, since 10 of 100 people with disease test negative. Sensitivity measures detected cases instead; the stated positive predictive value is correct.
options.misconception: Substitutes the missed-case fraction for the detected-case fraction.

options.label: E
options.text: Sensitivity 50%; probability of disease after a positive test 10%
options.explanation: Fifty percent is the positive predictive value, not sensitivity. Ten percent describes missed cases among people with disease, not the fraction of positive results that represent disease.
options.misconception: Confuses PPV and missed-case frequency with the requested measures.

explanation:
Learning objective: Use separate denominators for sensitivity and positive predictive value.

Sensitivity is 90 true positives divided by 100 people with disease, or 90%. Positive predictive value is 90 true positives divided by 180 positive results, or 50%.

evidence.title: Principles of Epidemiology (SS1978), Lesson 5 — Surveillance attributes

stem:
An independently classified sample contains 200 people with disease and 800 without disease. A test is positive in 160 people with disease and 80 without disease. An analyst reports 160/240 as specificity.

Which of the following calculations should replace that value?

options.label: A
options.explanation: This ratio measures sensitivity: detected cases divided by all people with disease. Specificity instead concerns correctly negative results among the independently identified group without disease.
options.misconception: Uses detection among diseased people to estimate specificity.

options.label: B
options.explanation: This is positive predictive value, because it divides true positives by all positive results. Specificity requires the disease-free group as the denominator and true negatives as the numerator.
options.misconception: Substitutes the positive-test denominator for the disease-free denominator.

options.label: C
options.explanation: This ratio asks what fraction of negative results come from people without disease. Specificity instead divides true negatives by all people without disease, including those who tested positive.
options.misconception: Confuses negative predictive value with specificity.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Among the 800 people without disease, 80 test positive and 720 test negative. Specificity is therefore 720/800, or 90%, using the disease-free group as its denominator.
options.misconception: No misconception: specificity counts true negatives among all noncases.

options.label: E
options.explanation: This ratio describes the fraction of the sample without disease. It does not assess whether the test correctly classified those people and therefore is not a measure of specificity.
options.misconception: Treats the proportion without disease as test classification accuracy.

explanation:
Learning objective: Calculate specificity from true negatives divided by all people without disease.

Among the 800 people without disease, 80 test positive and 720 test negative. Specificity is therefore 720/800, or 90%, using the disease-free group as its denominator.

stem:
A 50-year-old woman with type A blood inadvertently receives type B blood during surgery. Within minutes she develops fever, flank pain, and hypotension, and the transfusion is stopped immediately.

Which of the following best explains why this reaction began immediately, without any prior sensitization to type B cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Donor T lymphocytes attacked her tissues
options.explanation: Graft-versus-host reactions mediated by donor lymphocytes develop over days to weeks and cannot explain a reaction within minutes.
options.misconception: A delayed cellular reaction is being used to explain an immediate hemolytic one.

options.label: B
options.text: Her preformed anti-B antibodies bound the transfused cells
options.explanation: In contrast to antibodies against the Rh antigen, which are produced only after exposure, ABO group antibodies are preformed, so a type A recipient already carries anti-B antibodies that react immediately with donor B cells.
options.misconception: None; ABO isoagglutinins exist without prior exposure.

options.label: C
options.text: The donor blood contained high-titer anti-A antibodies
options.explanation: The dominant reaction is the recipient's preformed anti-B antibodies attacking transfused B cells; donor plasma antibodies are diluted and are not the principal driver.
options.misconception: The direction of antigen-antibody reactivity is being reversed.

options.label: D
options.text: Her plasma cells rapidly produced new anti-B antibodies
options.explanation: New antibody production after first exposure takes days; the immediate reaction implies antibodies that already existed.
options.misconception: A primary adaptive response is being credited with minute-level kinetics.

options.label: E
options.text: Complement was activated by transfused platelet antigens
options.explanation: ABO incompatibility targets erythrocyte antigens via preformed isoagglutinins; platelet antigens are not the basis of this immediate reaction.
options.misconception: The wrong cellular target is being implicated in an ABO reaction.

explanation: Learning objective: contrast ABO and Rh antibody kinetics. ABO antibodies are preformed, so incompatible transfusion reacts immediately; anti-Rh antibodies form only after exposure.

stem:
A 24-year-old medical student reviewing a normal ECG tracing identifies distinct deflections corresponding to atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization, and ventricular repolarization, but cannot find any deflection corresponding to atrial repolarization.

Which of the following best explains why this deflection is not seen?

options.label: A
options.text: Atrial repolarization generates no measurable electrical current
options.explanation: Repolarization is an electrical event and does generate current; the deflection exists but is buried in the contemporaneous QRS signal.
options.misconception: Absence of a deflection is being taken to mean absence of the electrical event.

options.label: B
options.text: It occurs after the T wave and is therefore not recorded
options.explanation: Atrial repolarization occurs during the QRS interval, well before the T wave (which reflects ventricular repolarization), and within the recorded tracing.
options.misconception: The timing of atrial repolarization is being placed outside the recorded cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: It is masked by the larger QRS complex at that moment
options.explanation: Atrial repolarization occurs at about the same time as ventricular depolarization, and its small signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex.
options.misconception: None; atrial repolarization coincides with ventricular depolarization and is hidden by it.

options.label: D
options.text: It is conducted too slowly through the atria to summate
options.explanation: The issue is not slow conduction but timing: the small atrial repolarization signal coincides with the dominant ventricular depolarization signal.
options.misconception: Conduction velocity is being blamed for a signal-amplitude problem.

options.label: E
options.text: The atria repolarize through a non-electrical mechanism
options.explanation: Repolarization of any myocardium is an electrical recovery process; it is hidden on the ECG rather than non-electrical.
options.misconception: Repolarization is being described as a mechanical rather than electrical process.

explanation: Learning objective: relate ECG deflections to electrical events. The P wave, QRS complex, and T wave correspond to atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization, and ventricular repolarization; atrial repolarization is masked by the QRS.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman stands up quickly from a supine position and experiences a transient decrease in arterial blood pressure, which is corrected within seconds and she does not faint.

Which of the following sequences correctly describes the immediate baroreceptor reflex response to this decrease in pressure?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased chemoreceptor firing, hyperventilation, increased pressure
options.explanation: Chemoreceptors monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH; the acute response to a postural pressure drop is mediated by baroreceptors, not ventilatory chemoreflexes.
options.misconception: The chemoreceptor reflex is being substituted for the baroreceptor reflex.

options.label: B
options.text: Increased baroreceptor firing, increased parasympathetic outflow via the vagus nerve, decreased heart rate
options.explanation: Increased firing with vagal slowing is the response to an increase in pressure; this patient's pressure fell, so firing decreases and sympathetic output rises instead.
options.misconception: The reflex response to rising pressure is being applied to falling pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased baroreceptor firing, increased vagal outflow, decreased heart rate
options.explanation: Although falling pressure does decrease firing, the reflex response to hypotension is sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal, which raise rather than lower the heart rate.
options.misconception: The afferent limb is correct but the efferent limb is inverted.

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased baroreceptor firing, increased sympathetic outflow, increased heart rate and vasoconstriction
options.explanation: Decreased blood pressure produces slower rates of baroreceptor firing; reduced afferent input increases sympathetic drive, raising heart rate and constricting peripheral vessels to restore pressure.
options.misconception: None; falling pressure slows baroreceptor firing, releasing sympathetic activation.

options.label: E
options.text: Increased atrial receptor firing, increased sympathetic firing, increased cardiac output
options.explanation: The atrial reflex responds to increased venous return and atrial stretch; standing reduces venous return transiently, and the correcting reflex is the arterial baroreceptor reflex.
options.misconception: The atrial (volume) reflex is being applied to an arterial pressure problem.

explanation: Learning objective: trace the baroreceptor reflex. Decreased pressure slows baroreceptor firing, increasing sympathetic output to raise heart rate and constrict vessels; the cardioinhibitor center acts via the vagus nerve when pressure rises.

stem:
A healthy 28-year-old medical student has a resting heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 mL. During a treadmill study, his cardiac output rises with exertion, as expected in a nonathlete, toward a maximum of about 20 L/min.

Which of the following values best approximates his resting cardiac output?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 70 beats per minute times 75 mL gives 5,250 mL/min, not half that value.
options.misconception: The stroke volume is being halved before multiplying by heart rate.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Outputs approaching 14-20 L/min occur during exercise, when rate and stroke volume both rise; the resting computation gives 5.25 L/min.
options.misconception: An exertional output is being reported as the resting value.

options.label: C
options.explanation: At 70 beats per minute, 7.0 L/min would require a stroke volume of 100 mL; with the measured 75 mL, output is 5.25 L/min.
options.misconception: A stroke volume of 100 mL is being assumed rather than the measured 75 mL.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Doubling either factor overestimates resting output; 70 × 75 mL yields 5.25 L/min, and values near 10 L/min belong to moderate exertion.
options.misconception: The resting rate is being doubled in the calculation.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 70 × 75 mL = 5,250 mL/min, or 5.25 L/min, the mean resting value cited for adults.
options.misconception: None; the computation matches the measured mean resting value.

explanation: Learning objective: compute cardiac output as heart rate times stroke volume. Resting output averages about 5.25 L/min and can rise toward 20 L/min in a nonathlete during exercise.

stem: When arterial blood pressure rises, baroreceptor firing rate most likely does which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreases because stretch receptors are inhibited by higher pressure
options.explanation: Baroreceptors increase firing when arterial pressure rises; decreased firing occurs when pressure falls.
options.misconception: The pressure–firing relationship is inverted.

options.label: B
options.text: Increases because greater vessel wall stretch activates the receptors
options.explanation: Increased blood pressure stretches carotid and aortic baroreceptors, producing increased rates of baroreceptor firing.
options.misconception: None; increased pressure raises baroreceptor firing rate.

options.label: C
options.text: No change because baroreceptors respond only to oxygen tension
options.explanation: Baroreceptors sense arterial stretch and pressure; chemoreceptors monitor blood gas and pH.
options.misconception: Chemoreceptor function is being substituted for baroreceptor function.

options.label: D
options.text: Complete cessation of firing until pressure normalizes
options.explanation: Baroreceptors fire continuously at a rate proportional to pressure; rising pressure increases, not abolishes, firing.
options.misconception: Baroreceptors are being treated as on–off switches rather than graded sensors.

options.label: E
options.text: Firing only during expiration when intrathoracic pressure rises
options.explanation: Carotid and aortic baroreceptors track arterial pressure continuously, not only during a respiratory phase.
options.misconception: A respiratory-cycle artifact is being confused with arterial baroreceptor behavior.

explanation: Learning objective: state the baroreceptor firing response to pressure. Increased blood pressure increases baroreceptor firing; decreased pressure slows firing.

stem: When a healthy person stands up quickly and arterial pressure falls transiently, baroreceptor afferent activity to the brainstem most likely does which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Increases, triggering increased parasympathetic outflow and bradycardia
options.explanation: Increased firing with vagal slowing follows a rise in pressure; when pressure falls, firing decreases instead.
options.misconception: The response to rising pressure is being applied to falling pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Decreases, reducing inhibitory input and permitting increased sympathetic outflow
options.explanation: Decreased blood pressure produces slower rates of baroreceptor firing; reduced afferent input permits increased sympathetic drive to raise heart rate and vascular tone.
options.misconception: None; slower firing releases sympathetic activation to restore pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Remains unchanged because chemoreceptors compensate within seconds
options.explanation: The immediate correction to an orthostatic pressure drop is mediated by baroreceptors, not ventilatory chemoreflexes.
options.misconception: Chemoreceptor reflexes are being substituted for the acute baroreceptor response.

options.label: D
options.text: Increases, causing reflex vasodilation in skeletal muscle beds
options.explanation: Falling pressure decreases, not increases, baroreceptor firing; the efferent response is sympathetic vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
options.misconception: Both the afferent direction and efferent limb are inverted.

options.label: E
options.text: Ceases entirely until venous return normalizes over several minutes
options.explanation: Baroreceptors continue firing at a reduced rate during hypotension; that reduced input triggers compensatory sympathetic activation within seconds.
options.misconception: Baroreceptors are being treated as silenced rather than firing more slowly.

explanation: Learning objective: apply the baroreceptor reflex to orthostasis. Falling pressure slows baroreceptor firing, releasing sympathetic activation that raises heart rate and constricts vessels.

stem:
A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension undergoes left heart catheterization with simultaneous phonocardiography and left ventricular pressure-volume recording. Immediately after the end of ejection, ventricular pressure falls rapidly while ventricular volume remains unchanged and no blood enters the ventricle. A sharp sound is recorded at the onset of this interval.

Which of the following valve events most directly produces this sound?

options.label: A
options.text: Simultaneous opening of all four heart valves
options.explanation: All four valves never open together in the normal cycle; the second heart sound is produced specifically by closure of the semilunar valves.
options.misconception: An impossible valve configuration is being proposed for a normal sound.

options.label: B
options.text: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
options.explanation: Mitral and tricuspid valve closure produces the first heart sound at the start of systole; the sound recorded after ejection ends reflects semilunar valve closure.
options.misconception: The onset-of-systole atrioventricular closure is being credited with the post-ejection sound.

options.label: C
options.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.explanation: When ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the end of systole, the semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound and beginning isovolumic relaxation with all valves shut.
options.misconception: None; semilunar valve closure marks the start of isovolumic relaxation and produces S2.

options.label: D
options.text: Opening of the atrioventricular valves during ventricular filling
options.explanation: Atrioventricular valves open silently during diastole when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; the audible event after ejection is semilunar closure.
options.misconception: A silent diastolic opening event is being substituted for an audible closure.

options.label: E
options.text: Opening of the semilunar valves at the start of ejection
options.explanation: Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure to begin ejection; the interval described follows ejection and ends with their closure.
options.misconception: The ejection-phase opening event is being placed at the post-ejection interval.

explanation: Learning objective: link S2 to isovolumic relaxation. After ejection, falling ventricular pressure closes the semilunar valves (S2), then both valve sets remain shut during isovolumic relaxation before atrioventricular valves reopen for filling.

stem: Which of the following equations defines cardiac output?

options.label: A
options.text: Heart rate divided by stroke volume
options.explanation: Cardiac output is the volume ejected per minute, so rate and stroke volume multiply; dividing would give beats per milliliter, not liters per minute.
options.misconception: The product relationship is being inverted.

options.label: B
options.text: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
options.explanation: Each beat ejects the stroke volume, and multiplying by heart rate gives total volume per minute — the definition of cardiac output.
options.misconception: None; cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume.

options.label: C
options.explanation: End-diastolic minus end-systolic volumes relate to stroke volume itself, not to the minute-by-minute output equation.
options.misconception: A chamber volume difference is being substituted for minute output.

options.label: D
options.text: Mean arterial pressure divided by systemic vascular resistance
options.explanation: That relationship links pressure, flow, and resistance; cardiac output is defined directly as heart rate times stroke volume.
options.misconception: A hemodynamic rearrangement is being confused with the pump definition.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Preload and afterload influence stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism, but cardiac output is heart rate times that stroke volume.
options.misconception: Load terms that modulate stroke volume are being multiplied as if they were the output formula.

explanation: Learning objective: state the cardiac output equation. Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume; resting values average about 5.25 L/min in adults.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with systolic heart failure has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25 percent. His resting heart rate is 88 beats per minute and stroke volume is 40 mL.

Which of the following values best approximates his resting cardiac output?

options.label: A
options.explanation: 7.0 L/min exceeds what 88 × 40 mL yields and is more typical of moderate exercise than decompensated resting failure.
options.misconception: An exertional output is being reported at rest.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Outputs near 14–20 L/min occur in vigorous exercise; resting failure with low stroke volume gives about 3.5 L/min.
options.misconception: Maximal exercise output is being chosen for a resting heart-failure patient.

options.label: C
options.explanation: 40 mL alone is not cardiac output; multiplying 88 beats per minute by 40 mL gives about 3.5 L/min.
options.misconception: Heart rate is being omitted from the product.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 88 × 40 mL = 3,520 mL/min ≈ 3.5 L/min, well below the normal resting average near 5.25 L/min in pump failure.
options.misconception: None; 88 × 40 mL ≈ 3.5 L/min.

options.label: E
options.explanation: 5.25 L/min would require a higher stroke volume or lower rate; with 40 mL per beat the product is about 3.5 L/min.
options.misconception: The population mean resting output is being applied despite low stroke volume.

explanation: Learning objective: compute low cardiac output in heart failure. Output = heart rate × stroke volume; with stroke volume 40 mL and rate 88/min, resting output is about 3.5 L/min.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction presents with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows elevated jugular venous pressure and bilateral crackles. Echocardiography reveals a dilated left ventricle with a markedly depressed ejection fraction. Despite an elevated end-diastolic volume, his forward stroke volume remains low.

Which of the following best explains why the Frank–Starling mechanism fails to restore adequate output in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased preload has abolished venous return to the heart
options.explanation: Venous return and preload are elevated; the problem is that the damaged myocardium cannot convert that stretch into an adequate stroke volume.
options.misconception: High filling is being treated as loss of venous return.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced contractility flattens the stretch–force relationship
options.explanation: Frank–Starling links greater stretch to stronger contraction only within limits and for a given inotropic state; after infarction, reduced contractility flattens that curve so elevated end-diastolic volume no longer yields adequate stroke volume.
options.misconception: None; a weak ventricle sits on a depressed Frank–Starling curve.

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased afterload prevents the ventricle from ejecting
options.explanation: Lower afterload would favor ejection; in systolic failure the limiting factor is reduced contractility, often with elevated afterload from vasoconstriction.
options.misconception: Low afterload is being blamed for low output.

options.label: D
options.text: Heart rate alone determines stroke volume in dilated ventricles
options.explanation: Heart rate multiplies stroke volume to give cardiac output; it does not replace preload–contractility coupling as the per-beat mechanism.
options.misconception: Rate is being substituted for the length–tension mechanism.

options.label: E
options.text: Increased ventricular compliance cancels any effect of stretch
options.explanation: Compliance affects how filling pressure maps to volume; the failed output here reflects depressed contractility on the Frank–Starling curve, not cancelled stretch from compliance alone.
options.misconception: A compliance change is being treated as the reason stretch fails.

explanation: Learning objective: recognize when Frank–Starling cannot compensate. In systolic heart failure, reduced contractility depresses the stretch–force curve so elevated preload no longer restores stroke volume.

stem: Mean arterial pressure is calculated by adding what fraction of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Adding two-thirds of the pulse pressure overweights systole; the correct weighting is one-third above diastolic.
options.misconception: Systolic pressure is being overweighted relative to diastolic.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Adding the full pulse pressure would approximate systolic pressure, not the time-averaged mean.
options.misconception: The entire systolic-diastolic difference is being added to diastolic.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero — MAP equals diastolic pressure alone
options.explanation: Diastolic pressure alone ignores systolic flow during systole; one-third of the pulse pressure must be added.
options.misconception: The contribution of systolic pressure during systole is being ignored entirely.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Diastole lasts longer than systole, so the mean is weighted toward diastolic pressure; one-half would equal the simple midpoint, not MAP.
options.misconception: The arithmetic midpoint of systolic and diastolic is being used instead of the time-weighted mean.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Mean arterial pressure equals diastolic pressure plus one-third of the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures.
options.misconception: None; MAP equals diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure.
